FULL VIEW
OUTLINE VIEW
Pretest
Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Understand the etiology and natural history of complex regional pain syndrome, including risk
factors.
Recognize clinical findings and diagnostic studies that support the diagnosis of complex
regional pain syndrome.
Specify options for the prevention and management of complex regional pain syndrome.
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Overview
Complex regional pain syndrome (CRPS) is characterized by chronic, localized pain typically
involving one extremity.
Usually occurs after an injury, most commonly a fracture

Sometimes the injury is seemingly innocuous, or the pain may occur without injury.
May occur after elective surgery
Characterized by disproportionate pain associated with trophic changes
The underlying pathophysiology is a complex interaction of multiple systems.
Specific criteria for diagnosis have been developed; however, CRPS should always be
considered a diagnosis of exclusion.
Epidemiology
Upper extremity fracture is the most common inciting event1-5.
More common in women than in men
Incidence of 3.8% to 7% in the 4 months after a fracture reported in two prospective studies1,4
(Resources 1, 2, 3, and 4).
Genetic predisposition is based on association with specific human leukocyte antigen (HLA)
subtypes.
Association with psychiatric disorders is unclear.

Epidemiology
Upper extremity fractures are the most common inciting event; however, CRPS can occur
after a mild injury or elective surgery in any extremity and has been described in
patients without identifiable trauma. Two large population studies have been
performed, one in Scandinavia, which estimated the incidence of CRPS at 26.2 per
100,000 person-years, and another in Olmsted County, Minnesota, which reported an
incidence of 5.46 per 100,000 person-years.2,6 CRPS is far more common in females,
with a relative risk between 3.4 and 42.6 CRPS is most prevalent in postmenopausal
women. The disease is most common in the middle decades of life and is rare but has
been described in children and elderly individuals. Association with HLA typing suggests
a genetic predisposition for CRPS.7
Historically, any underlying psychiatric diagnosis was thought to increase the risk of
CRPS. Axis type I disorders, mainly major depression, have been reported in 24% to 49%
of patients with CRPS, which is consistent with other chronic pain syndromes.1 A

prospective, multicenter cohort study evaluated 596 patients with fractures and
collected baseline psychological data. Although CRPS occurred in 7.0% of the patients, no
association with baseline psychological factors was reported.8
Pathophysiology
Multifactorial; exact mechanism poorly understood
Central and peripheral nervous system sensitization leads to atypical responses to nociceptive
stimuli.1,3,5
Sympathetic nervous system alterations may result from autoantibodies to adrenergic and
muscarinic receptors.3
Atypical proinflammatory and immunologic responses lead to changes in B cell activation and
increased interleukin 1 beta, substance P, and osteoprotegerin.1,9
Changes occur in peripheral nerve innervation, including fiber subtypes and autonomic
systems.3-5
Brain plasticity plays a role.1
Genetic association with HLA subtypes suggests abnormal regulation of inflammation and
neuroplasticity.7

Pathophysiology
Multifactorial mechanisms result in CRPS, and the exact mechanism is poorly
understood. A single pathophysiologic pathway has not emerged, suggesting that
multiple mechanisms likely exist. Atypical proinflammatory and immunologic responses
to the triggering injury appear to initiate the process.
After initial injury, peripheral sensitization develops with local proinflammatory peptides,
increased background firing, and a decreased firing threshold in response to normal
nociceptive stimuli. Mediators involved in peripheral sensitization are increased,
including changes in B cell activation and increased interleukin 1 beta, substance P, and
osteoprotegerin. Sympathoafferent coupling may result from increased catecholamine
receptors on nociceptive fibers, leading to atypical pain.1 The relationship to the long-
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:42 AM
AAOS | Complex Regional Pain Syndrome
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001018
3/27

term clinical picture of exaggerated sympathetic response is less clearly understood.1
Changes in peripheral nerve innervation include decreases in the density of fiber
subtypes, abnormal innervation around hair follicles and sweat glands, and changes in
autonomic systems.3-5 Sympathetic nervous system alterations may result from
autoantibodies to adrenergic and muscarinic receptors.3
Central nervous system sensitization leads to atypical responses to nociceptive stimuli.
Brain plasticity also appears to be involved, with reduced representation of the affected
limb on primary and secondary somatosensory cortices and disinhibition of the primary
motor cortex.1
Other identified immunologic system mechanisms include increased numbers of CD14+,
CD16+ and mast cells and impaired neutrophil activity.1 Genetic association with HLA
subtypes suggests abnormal regulation of inflammation and neuroplasticity.7
Natural History
Symptoms of CRPS typically develop between weeks and 3 to 4 months after the initiating
injury.
In the early phase, the patient often has a warm, red, edematous limb (warm CRPS) reflecting
inflammatory symptoms.1
In the later phase, the patient often has a cool, blue limb (cold CRPS), representing a transition
to predominately autonomic features1 (Figure 1).
Spontaneous resolution is the typical outcome for acute CRPS, with most symptoms resolving
within a year of onset.1,3,6
A systematic review from 2014 found that most patients with CRPS recover within 6 to 13
months; however, those with a longer duration of CRPS had more severe symptoms. The
authors of the study noted the poor quality of evidence.10
Anxiety, pain-related fear, and disability are associated with poorer outcomes, and CRPS may
be associated with a higher risk of suicide.1,11

the right lower limb that was obtained approximately 15 months after internal fixation of an
ankle fracture and the onset of complex regional pain syndrome shows abnormal skin
coloration and hair growth. A healed incision is visible ventral to the medial malleolus. The
patient has mild-to-moderate stiffness of the ankle and severe stiffness of the toes.
(Reproduced with permission from Koh TT, Daly A, Howard W, Tan C, Hardidge A: Complex
regional pain syndrome. JBJS Rev 2014;2[7]:e5.) 

Natural History
Historically, acute, dystrophic, and atrophic phases were identified based on physical
findings.12 Currently, this classification is used less commonly because changes can
occur at any stage.10,13 Differentiating warm and cold CRPS may have prognostic value
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:42 AM
AAOS | Complex Regional Pain Syndrome
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001018
5/27

because patients with the more common warm symptoms of inflammation may be more
likely to have resolution of the process, whereas patients with cold symptoms have
poorer clinical pain outcomes.14
The vasomotor and sudomotor symptoms more common in the early stages are most
likely to resolve, whereas motor symptoms of weakness and stiffness are most likely to
persist.10
A meta-analysis by Bean et al10 summarized multiple prognostic factors predicting a
poor outcome with CRPS, including longer pain duration, more intense pain, delayed
management, younger patient age, more severe fracture, power grip strength, and lower
mobility. Conversely, studies noted improved outcomes in patients with a fracture as the
inciting event, absence of sensory symptoms, the presence of swelling, single joint
involvement, a warm limb in the early stages, and no delay between injury and the onset
of CRPS. Although underlying psychiatric diagnosis remains an unclear risk factor,
studies have demonstrated that anxiety, pain-related fear, disability, and psychological
distress may contribute to intensity of symptoms and overall poorer outcome, including
higher risk of suicide.1,11
Risk Factors
Inciting event of trauma or surgery
Prior diagnosis of CRPS greatly increases the risk of CRPS after a second injury or surgery.15
Underlying psychiatric disorders1,11
Genetic predisposition in HLA-DQ8 and HLA-B627
Incidence of 4.36% after foot and ankle surgery16
CRPS has been described as a complication after multiple elective foot and ankle procedures,
including hammer toe correction, bunion correction, midfoot fusion, subtalar fusion, ankle
open reduction and internal fixation, ankle arthroscopy, ankle arthrodesis, total ankle
arthroplasty.12,17-27


Risk Factors
An inciting injury is almost universal in the development of CRPS; however, CRPS has
been reported to occur spontaneously.2 Although upper extremity involvement is more
common than lower extremity involvement, a review of foot and ankle surgeries
reported an incidence of 4.36%, and CRPS frequently is included among complications of
foot and ankle surgery. Bullen et al16 noted a much lower incidence (0.3%) than previous
studies after ankle fractures, using rigorous diagnosis via the Budapest criteria. Although
the numbers were small, the authors postulated that CRPS may be over-diagnosed.
Satteson et al15 found a 75% rate of CRPS after a second injury in a small cohort of
retrospectively reviewed patients with a previous diagnosis of CRPS. Elective surgery
should be approached with caution in patients with a history of CRPS.
Classification
CRPS type I: historically reflex sympathetic dystrophy; no confirmed nerve injury
CRPS type II: historically causalgia; confirmed nerve injury is present

Classification
The term complex regional pain syndrome was introduced after a consensus workshop
in 1994 as a general, descriptive name associated with standardized diagnostic criteria28
to clarify the condition. Other historical terms for the condition include algodystrophy,
algoneurodystrophy, posttraumatic dystrophy, Sudeck atrophy, and sympathetically
mediated pain syndrome.3,12,13
In CRPS type -I, the diagnostic criteria are met in the absence of a confirmed peripheral
nerve injury. In type II CRPS , signs and symptoms are present with a confirmed
peripheral nerve injury. Of historical interest, CRPS–not otherwise specified was included
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:42 AM
AAOS | Complex Regional Pain Syndrome
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001018
7/27

to capture patients previously diagnosed with CRPS but not meeting the Budapest
criteria if symptoms could not be explained by another diagnosis.13
Evaluation/Diagnosis

Evaluation/Diagnosis
CRPS should be considered a diagnosis of exclusion that is made via a patient history
and a physical examination. Using the objective criteria, including the criterion that no
other diagnosis is more likely, is crucial to avoid overdiagnosis. Imaging studies are
important to rule out other diagnoses rather than to confirm or refute a diagnosis of
CRPS.
Diagnosis
Current diagnostic criteria were refined by the 2003 Budapest consensus conference and
subsequently validated4,13,16,28-30 (Resource 4).
Pain described is out of proportion to that expected for an injury, failing to diminish with time.
No other diagnosis can better explain the signs and symptoms.
On history, the patient must have a complaint of at least one symptom in at least three of the
following categories:
Sensory: allodynia and/or hyperesthesia
Vasomotor: changes/asymmetry in skin color or temperature
Sudomotor/vascular: edema and/or sweating changes/asymmetry
Motor/trophic: decreased range of motion and/or motor dysfunction (weakness, tremor,
dystonia) and/or trophic changes of hair, skin, nails
Physical examination requires at least one physical sign in two or more of the following
categories:
Sensory: hyperalgesia to pinprick and/or allodynia (to light touch, temperature, deep
pressure, and/or joint motion)
Vasomotor: temperature asymmetry greater than 33.8°F (1°C) and/or skin color change or
asymmetry

Sudomotor/vascular: edema and/or sweating changes/asymmetry
Motor/trophic: decreased range of motion and/or motor dysfunction (weakness, tremor,
dystonia) and/or trophic changes of hair, skin, nails
Patient History

Patient History
The patient may report a history of injury, fracture, or elective surgery as the inciting
event leading to pain isolated to a single extremity of greater intensity and duration than
expected. The quality of pain may be deep aching, burning, stabbing, shooting, or jolting.
Typically, pain is worse with any movement or weight bearing. The description of pain
includes allodynia (pain from normally non-noxious stimuli, such as light touch or water
falling on the skin); hyperalgesia (disproportionate pain from a noxious stimulus, such as
severe pain from a pinprick); abnormal vasomotor activity, such as limb swelling and
color change; and abnormal motor function, such as weakness, spasms, or dystonia.
History of a nerve injury may be noted.
The patient should be asked about any previous diagnosis of CRPS and underlying
psychiatric or psychological disorders that may affect prognosis.
Physical Examination
Observation: color changes of red or blue, brawny discoloration in late stages, loss of hair
growth, atrophy and swelling (Figure 2)
Palpation: temperature changes, hyperhidrosis (more typically) or anhidrosis and/or edema
Range of motion: reduced active and passive motion, possible joint contractures
Motor testing: weakness, possible tremors or dystonia
Sensory testing: allodynia, hyperalgesia, pain with thermal stimuli3

Figure 2 AP (A) and lateral (B) radiographs of the right foot of a middle-aged woman obtained 3
months after open reduction and fixation of a talar neck fracture. The patient had pain in the
entire foot and stiffness of the ankle and all the joints. The patient was not able to tolerate
bearing weight or wearing shoes. The amount of osteopenia observed is beyond that expected
from disuse, which is a finding typical of the dystrophic stage. (Reproduced from Hogan CJ,


Physical Examination
Physical examination of a limb affected by CRPS may be a challenge. Allodynia and fear
of pain may produce withdrawal or inability to tolerate palpation or manipulation.
Comparison with the contralateral limb is important. Observation may demonstrate
trophic changes with atrophic skin and/or loss of hair growth. Vascular changes produce
discolored skin ranging from blue to red. Patients with chronic CRPS may have atrophic,
shiny skin or brawny discoloration. Palpation should reveal findings consistent with
autonomic dysfunction: a limb that is warmer or cooler than the contralateral limb, with
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:42 AM
AAOS | Complex Regional Pain Syndrome
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001018
10/27

hyperhidrosis (more typically) or anhidrosis. Swelling or edema frequently is present.
Range of motion may be profoundly restricted because of pain, apprehension, or (in
later stages) joint contractures. Motor testing will reveal weakness but also more global
atrophy and dysfunction with tremors or dystonia. Sensory testing may be notable for
allodynia, and hyperalgesia and for pain induced by thermal stimuli.4,5,13,30
Trevino et al31 described the kick-off sign, in which the patient holds the affected limb in
knee extension on the examination table. In a large case study, this finding was
consistent with lower extremity CRPS. Resolution of this physical examination findings
was associated with resolution of all symptoms.31
Imaging Studies
Radiography: nonspecific; may demonstrate osteopenia, cortical resorption32 (Figure 3)
MRI: may be helpful in identifying occult fractures but is not an effective screening or
diagnostic imaging study13,32
Bone scintigraphy: higher sensitivity than MRI, with similar specificity31(Figure 4)

Imaging Studies

Imaging studies for CRPS should begin with radiographs to define an existing injury or
evaluate for an undiagnosed bone injury. Osteopenia or periarticular resorption may be
present because of disuse but is not diagnostic. Advanced imaging studies, particularly
MRI, should be considered to identify occult injuries. Because of typical vascular
changes, the specificity of MRI is high with regard to the diagnosis of CRPS (atypical
findings will be present on MRI in most patients with CRPS). The signal pattern may
resemble findings present in patients with inflammatory, traumatic, or postoperative
processes; therefore, the sensitivity of MRI is poor, and it should not be used for
diagnostic purposes.13,32 The increased vascularity observed in patients with CRPS leads
to diffuse uptake on all phases of a three-phase bone scan. Bone scintigraphy is
associated with better sensitivity (up high as 100%) in patients with CRPS of the foot and
ankle, with 80% specificity.32
Differential Diagnosis
Fibromyalgia4,13
Nerve entrapment
Peripheral neuropathy
Compartment syndrome
Peripheral artery disease
Raynaud disease
Lymphatic obstruction/deep vein thrombosis
Infection
Inflammatory arthritis
Munchausen syndrome/malingering

Differential Diagnosis
Because CRPS is a diagnosis of exclusion, a broad range of differential diagnoses should
be considered and rejected before CRPS is accepted as the definitive diagnosis

14/27

Prevention
Vitamin C has been demonstrated to reduce the risk of CRPS in multiple studies, including
systematic reviews and meta-analyses.32-35 and a prospective randomized study.36

Prevention
The putative mechanism for vitamin C is that the antioxidant properties decrease the
acute inflammatory response to the stress of injury or surgery.4 A meta-analysis by Chen
et al33 rreviewed studies on general postoperative pain, including six studies on type I
CRPS. Most studies on vitamin C supplementation have used a model of distal radius or
upper extremity injuries; however, vitamin C supplementation also has been shown to
be effective in patients with foot and ankle injury or patients undergoing foot and ankle
surgery.34-35,37In a prospective, randomized study of patients undergoing elective or
trauma foot and ankle surgery, Hernigou et al36 reported that 1 gram of vitamin C
supplementation per day for 40 days decreased the risk of CRPS.
Management

Management
Management of CRPS remains mostly empirical. The concept of functional restoration
has been promulgated to achieve a holistic approach to the management of CRPS.13
Many studies of treatment options have been published, including multiple Cochrane
reviews; however, most studies have been small and/or of limited quality.
Nonsurgical Management
Physical Therapy

15/27

Has been considered the primary treatment option, but efficacy has not been demonstrated in
high-quality studies368
Physical therapy should involve a progressive program as pain symptoms and fear allow.
Graded motor imagery and use of mirror therapy may improve CRPS outcomes (Figure 5).
Figure 5 Clinical photographs show mirror visual feedback of the lower (A) and upper (B) limbs.
With the affected limb hidden from view, the patient observes the reflected image of the
nonaffected limb in the mirror. (Reproduced with permission from Koh TT, Daly A, Howard W, Tan
C, Hardidge A: Complex regional pain syndrome. JBJS Rev 2014;2[7]:e5.)

Physical Therapy
Despite the lack of high-quality studies, early referral for physical therapy is important to
address pain and promote return of function. Physical therapy should be individualized
and should be initiated early, beginning with mobilization and desensitization. Passive
range of motion should be used with caution because it may exacerbate symptoms.12 As
symptoms allow, progression to edema control, including the use of an edema-
controlling device, and massage should be initiated. Improvement of flexibility via
isometric strengthening is followed by isotonic strengthening, progression of weight
bearing, and more aggressive range of motion.5,13,30

Mirror therapy is associated with good results in patients with early or intermediate-
stage CRPS, including patients with lower extremity involvement but was not effective in
patients with late-stage disease who had trophic changes.39 Graded motor imagery
includes staged visualization before recruitment of the affected limb and shows
potential for reducing pain.38
Medication
NSAIDs can be used for analgesia.
Oral steroids may be effective, particularly in the acute inflammatory phase.
Low-dose naltrexone has been shown to be effective in limited studies.
Gabapentin, tricyclic antidepressants, and carbamazepine may afford symptom relief.
Calcitonin and alendronate appear to improve pain, motor, and trophic symptoms.
Ketamine may afford short-term relief.
Intrathecal baclofen demonstrated efficacy for dystonia associated with CRPS.
Although low-morphine equivalent opioids (tramadol) have been shown to effectively manage
neuropathic pain, including CRPS, in some studies, other studies have not demonstrated
efficacy.40

Medication
Multiple medications for CRPS have been studied, some in trials involving a broader
diagnosis of neuropathic pain. The use of NSAIDs is low risk and may provide analgesia41
Oral steroids are supported in low-quality studies. Gabapentin has shown efficacy in
several studies (including a level I study); however, it was not supported in a Cochrane
review.38,42 Tricyclic antidepressants also may afford relief.42,43
Recently, low-dose naltrexone has been explored for the management of CRPS. Low-
dose naltrexone, which is a reversible competitive antagonist at the mu and kappa
opioid receptors, is advantageous because it is an inexpensive medication with a low risk
for adverse events.44 A systematic review reported encouraging results with the use of
low-dose naltrexone for the management CRPS; however, the use of low-dose
SEND FEEDBACK

AAOS | Complex Regional Pain Syndrome
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001018
17/27

naltrexone is predominantly supported by retrospective studies performed outside of
the United States.45
The use of ketamine as a topical cream was reported effective in a case report;46
however, a level I study demonstrated only short-term improvement if a multiday
ketamine infusion was used for management of CRPS.47 Intrathecal baclofen
demonstrated efficacy for dystonia associated with CRPS.47
Calcitonin and alendronate are successful for the management of symptoms of pain,
immobility, osteopenia, and trophic changes.38,49
Given the opioid crisis, use of this class of medications should be approached carefully. A
Cochrane review demonstrated efficacy of tramadol for the management of neuropathic
pain.38 Studies on the use of opioids specifically in patients with CRPS are limited. A level
I study comparing the use of carbamazepine and morphine with spinal cord stimulators
showed efficacy of carbamazepine but not morphine.40
Injections
Lumbar sympathetic blocks with local anesthesia may be effective in some patients.
Intravenous regional sympathetic blocks with guanethidine are not recommended because of
poor efficacy and adverse events.50

Injections
Historically, local anesthetic sympathetic blocks have been used diagnostically and
therapeutically5,12 however, data have not supported their effectiveness.5,51 A 2016
Cochrane review reported limited, low-quality publications demonstrating minimal or no
difference with sympathetic blocks;50 however, a study with botulinum A suggested
longer duration of relief.52

The single clear recommendation from a 2016 Cochrane review on the management of
CRPS was against the use of intravenous regional blockade with guanethidine because of
lack of efficacy and the risk of adverse events.50
Psychotherapy
CRPS is not a primary psychiatric disorder; however, psychotherapy plays an important
adjunctive role to address anxiety.
Surgical Management
Spinal Cord Stimulators

Spinal Cord Stimulators
Stimulation of the dorsal root ganglion with implantable electrodes is used to manage
chronic pain, including CRPS refractory to other treatment modalities. Spinal cord
stimulation evolved from gate control theory of nociceptive signals. The mechanism of
action is stimulation of the A beta fibers in the dorsal column, altering the painful signals
in the A delta and C fibers.53
A 2000 trial by Kemler et al54 found improvement if electrode implantation in the spinal
cord was combined with physical therapy;. however, 5-year follow-up of the cohort
demonstrated no sustained improvement compared with the group that received
physical therapy alone.55 In addition, 42% of patients experienced some complication
with the implant during the follow-up period. A case series demonstrated a mean of 53%
improvement in pain relief on a visual analog scale.13 A study on the use of spinal cord
stimulation earlier in the course of CRPS concluded that early use is unlikely to provide
benefit over use for the management of chronic CRPS.56 A systematic literature review
demonstrated high-level evidence for a positive effect of spinal cord stimulation on pain
relief, pain score, and quality of life in patients with CRPS; however, the authors noted a
lack of evidence to support other functional improvements.57 A recent consensus paper

recommended dorsal root ganglion stimulation as an effective therapy for the
management type I or type II CRPS.58
Sympathectomy

Sympathectomy
Sympathectomy in patients responding well to a sympathetic block has been described;
however, success has been variable, with studies reporting that residual pain is likely,
and risks should be considered.5,12,38 A 2013 Cochrane review found little high-quality
evidence to support the technique and concluded that sympathectomy should be used
with caution.59
Amputation

Amputation
Amputation seems an extreme treatment option, but it may be an option for
management of persistent, refractory CRPS. A 2019 systematic review that included eight
studies supported amputation for patients with the most refractory CRPS. The pooled
results were based on 96 patients. The authors noted that 68% of the patients
experienced improved quality of life; however, quality of life deteriorated for 28%of the
patients. Recurrence of CRPS occurred in 46% of the patients.60
A study that was included in the systematic review reported outcomes for 21 of 22
patients at a mean follow-up of 5 years after amputation for the management of type I
CRPS. In this study, 15 patients underwent lower-limb amputation, 10 of whom regularly
used a prosthesis. The authors reported that 95% of the patients reported overall
improvement in their lives, with 90% experiencing pain reduction; however, 24% of the
patients experienced recurrence of CRPS symptoms in the residual limb or in another
limb.61 The authors recommended amputation for management of type I CRPS resistant

to other therapies in patients with no major psychopathology and a realistic
understanding of the risks and advantages of amputation.
An earlier review of the literature included 111 amputations in 107 patients. CRPS
recurred in 31 of 65 patients, and 14 patients had phantom pain.62 The same authors
subsequently reported on an informed decision-making model to guide amputation,
noting the lack of studies to guide decision making on amputation level, and
recommended amputation above the level of allodynia.63
